Herein, the materials were prepared using a medium-frequency induction furnace and atmospheric melting.
The alloy ingot was then homogenized at 950 ◦C for 12 h and then forged.
The optimal thermal working parameters were achieved at 950 ◦C and 1 s 1, and the size of the forged alloy sheet was 200 mm × 160 mm × 8 mm.
First, the forged alloy underwent a solid-solution treatment by being held at 950 ◦C for 3 h.
Subsequently, the solid solution alloy was cold-rolled to achieve 87.5% deformation.
Following this, an annealing treatment was conducted at 300 ◦C for 2 h, followed by furnace cooling.
The annealed alloy was subsequently subjected to cold rolling with a 50% deformation, resulting in a 0.5-mm-thick copper alloy sheet.
The obtained alloy was then subjected to 2-h aging at 450 ◦C to obtain the test material.

evidence.section: 4.1 Microstructure analysis of the aged alloy
evidence.quote: After the deformation and heat treatment of the Cu – 1.16Ni – 0.36Cr alloy, dispersed nanoscale precipitates are present within the alloy matrix ( Fig. 8 (a and b)).
Microstructural analysis revealed the formation of nanoscale Ni3Cr7 precipitates near fractures at high temperatures, with the average size being approximately 10 nm.

evidence.section: 4.1 Microstructure analysis of the aged alloy
evidence.quote: The majority of grain boundary angles in the alloy were concentrated in the range of small-angle grain boundaries, with small-angle grain boundaries accounting for 83.1% of the total grain-boundary proportion in the alloy.

The relation between the grain boundaries and the precipitates is referred to as the “ bypass mechanism, ” which substantially enhances the alloy strength.
Furthermore, the precipitate was more distributed in regions where dislocations gather, effectively impeding dislocation movement and improving the strength of the alloy.
